schema.title: Response History Api Rider Trips Get

ActionOutcomeResponse.title: ActionOutcomeResponse
ActionOutcomeResponse.description:
What was observed after an approved action ran.

Observation, not attribution: there is no holdout group, so these are orders
that *used* the offer, not orders the offer can be shown to have caused.

ActionOutcomeVerdict.title: ActionOutcomeVerdict
ActionOutcomeVerdict.description:
What was observed after an action ran.

Deliberately phrased as observation, not causation: there is no holdout
group, so nothing here can prove the action produced the result.

AdminCommissionReport.title: AdminCommissionReport
AdminCommissionReport.description: What the platform earned, per restaurant, over a window.

AdminUserResponse.title: AdminUserResponse
AdminUserResponse.description:
A user row for the admin console, with the app it belongs to.

Customers are scoped to one app client; `app_label` is what the console
shows. Platform staff (ADMIN/OWNER) have no app client, so every app field
is null and the console renders them as platform accounts.

AdminUserStats.title: AdminUserStats
AdminUserStats.description: Accounts per role, for the tiles above the Users list.

AdminUserUpdate.title: AdminUserUpdate
AdminUserUpdate.description:
Editable customer details.

Email is deliberately absent: it is half of the per-app login identity
(`uq_users_app_client_id_email_customer`), so changing it here would
silently change who can sign in to the account.

AppClientResponse.title: AppClientResponse
AppClientResponse.description: Flattened view of an app client and its PROD platform identifiers.

AppClientUpsertRequest.title: AppClientUpsertRequest
AppClientUpsertRequest.description:
Full app client configuration for an existing restaurant.

Every field is required: the admin edit form always submits the complete
configuration, and restaurants without an app client get one created here.

AppConfigResponse.title: AppConfigResponse
AppConfigResponse.description:
Startup configuration a mobile build resolves from its own bundle ID.

`restaurant_id` is null for `MARKETPLACE` apps, which browse every
restaurant, and set for `SINGLE_RESTAURANT` apps, which are scoped to one.

AttentionFlagResponse.title: AttentionFlagResponse
AttentionFlagResponse.description:
Something the owner should look at, phrased as the thing to do.

`id` is stable per kind so the Hub can key its carousel without the flags
reordering underneath it between refreshes.

BranchLocationLookup.title: BranchLocationLookup
BranchLocationLookup.description:
What a geocoder made of a branch's own address.

Every field but `found` exists so a person can judge the answer before
saving it. A geocoder always answers something, so "it returned a
coordinate" is not evidence that it found the right building — `precise`
and `matched` are what make the difference visible.

BrandFaqPayload.title: BrandFaqPayload
BrandFaqPayload.description: One question a customer asks before a first order, and its answer.

BrandHighlightPayload.title: BrandHighlightPayload
BrandHighlightPayload.description: One figure worth putting in a band, and where it came from.

BrandSectionPayload.title: BrandSectionPayload
BrandSectionPayload.description: One headed section of what a restaurant says about itself.

CampaignContentSchema.title: CampaignContentSchema
CampaignContentSchema.description:
What the customer sees, in the shape the chosen channel needs.

`title` and `body` are the two fields every channel has some version of -
a push title and body, an email subject and message, a WhatsApp header and
text - so they stay columns. `extra` is everything that belongs to one or
two channels only: the photo a post cannot exist without, a hashtag block,
a boost budget, the promo code a public post is attributed by.

It is carried, not interpreted. The backend stores it and hands it back
unchanged, which is what lets a new channel ship as a frontend change plus
a dispatcher, with no migration and no schema edit here. Push - the only
channel that sends today - reads nothing from it.

Size-capped rather than typed per key, because the alternative is this
schema growing a branch per channel and every addition becoming a backend
release. The cap is what stops it being used as a document store.

CampaignDraftRequest.title: CampaignDraftRequest
CampaignDraftRequest.description:
A save from any step of the wizard.

Deliberately permissive: a draft is saved continuously as the owner moves
through six steps, and refusing to persist a half-finished one would mean
losing their work every time they stepped away. Everything that makes a
campaign *sendable* is validated at send time instead, where it can be
re-checked against data that may have moved since the draft was written.

CampaignEngagementRequest.title: CampaignEngagementRequest
CampaignEngagementRequest.description: What a device reports a customer did with a campaign it received.

CartActionResponse.title: CartActionResponse
CartActionResponse.description:
One cart change the ordering agent decided on, as the wire sees it.

Identifiers and a quantity, and deliberately nothing else: the client
already has the branch menu loaded and renders the name and the price from
that, so putting either here would create a second source for them that can
disagree with the menu the customer is looking at. `status` is the field
that matters most — `proposed` means the client must ASK before changing
anything, and every destructive change is proposed by construction.

CartLinePayload.title: CartLinePayload
CartLinePayload.description:
What the browser says is in the cart.

Identifiers only, and treated as untrusted: the service re-resolves every
id against the selected branch and ignores whatever does not belong there.
Names and prices are never taken from here.

ChannelConnectRequest.title: ChannelConnectRequest
ChannelConnectRequest.description:
What the owner typed into the connect form.

An open map rather than a field per channel: the fields differ per
channel and are declared in `connections.REQUIREMENTS`, which is also
what validates this. A schema per channel would be five schemas that have
to be kept in step with that map.

ChannelConnectionResponse.title: ChannelConnectionResponse
ChannelConnectionResponse.description:
One channel's state for one restaurant.

Carries `config` and never `credentials`. That split is the whole reason
the model has two JSONB columns: an owner needs to see which number they
are sending from, and nobody needs the token that sends from it.

ChannelConnectionStatus.title: ChannelConnectionStatus
ChannelConnectionStatus.description:
How far a restaurant has got with switching a channel on.

Absence of a row means NOT_CONNECTED, so this enum never needs that value:
a status column that can disagree with the existence of the row it sits on
is a bug waiting to be written.

DISABLED is distinct from deleting the row. An owner who pauses WhatsApp
for a month should not have to re-authorise Meta afterwards, and a channel
that failed verification should keep its configuration so the owner can
see what was wrong with it.

ChargeLineResponse.title: ChargeLineResponse
ChargeLineResponse.description:
One row of the breakdown behind the collapsed charges line.

`note` is not decoration. A platform fee with no explanation reads as a
made-up number, and a tax row that does not say the rate is the
government's invites a complaint aimed at the wrong party.

ChatPlaceOrderRequest.title: ChatPlaceOrderRequest
ChatPlaceOrderRequest.description:
Place the order this conversation has been building.

Carries no contact details: those were collected and validated over the
conversation and live in the draft this session owns. All that is needed
here is which conversation, which branch, and the cart the browser is
holding — the same cart every other ordering call sends.

ChatThreadLine.title: ChatThreadLine
ChatThreadLine.description:
One line of the thread as the customer saw it. Text only, capped: it
feeds a prompt, never a database row.

ConnectionFieldResponse.title: ConnectionFieldResponse
ConnectionFieldResponse.description:
One thing the owner has to supply before a channel can send.

`secret` is here so the form can render a password input and, more
importantly, so it can show an existing connection's non-secret values
while leaving the secret blank — a stored token cannot be displayed, and
re-saving without retyping it must not blank it.

CurrencyResponse.title: CurrencyResponse
CurrencyResponse.description: A currency as a client needs it to format money.

DeliveryQuoteRequest.title: DeliveryQuoteRequest
DeliveryQuoteRequest.description:
Where to, so a courier can price the trip.

Deliberately not the whole cart. A customer typing their address wants to
know the delivery fee before they have finished choosing food, and making
them assemble a valid order first to learn the price is the wrong way
round.

DeliveryQuoteResponse.title: DeliveryQuoteResponse
DeliveryQuoteResponse.description:
What delivery costs, and where the figure came from.

`source` is the point of this response. A checkout showing a number the
customer will pay should be able to say whether a courier priced this
particular trip or whether it is the restaurant's own flat rate — and a
support call six weeks later is unanswerable without it.

DeliverySimulateRequest.title: DeliverySimulateRequest
DeliverySimulateRequest.description: A sandbox stage, as Pidge's `dummy_status` names it.

DeliveryStep.title: DeliveryStep
DeliveryStep.description: One thing the courier reported, as it reported it.

GuestPreferencePayload.title: GuestPreferencePayload
GuestPreferencePayload.description:
Durable traits a browser is carrying for a visitor with no account.

Honoured ONLY for a guest. For an authenticated user the database is the
only source and this is ignored outright — see `resolve_chat_preferences`.
Both values are re-normalised server-side, so anything unrecognised becomes
None rather than reaching a query.

InsightsDataQuality.title: InsightsDataQuality
InsightsDataQuality.description: Caveats a narrator must surface rather than quietly paper over.

KitchenStaffUpdate.title: KitchenStaffUpdate
KitchenStaffUpdate.description:
What may be changed after the fact.

Deliberately not the email or the password: re-pointing an existing login
at a different person is how a revoked account quietly comes back. Deactivate
and create another.

KitchenStockUpdate.title: KitchenStockUpdate
KitchenStockUpdate.description:
Only what is sent changes. Sending `stock_quantity: null` stops
counting; leaving it out keeps the count — the editor-left-open-while-
three-sold problem `frontend-admin/src/services/menuStock.ts` describes.

LiveOrderResponse.title: LiveOrderResponse
LiveOrderResponse.description:
An order as a card on the live board: the order, and its courier.

`delivery` is null for a pickup order and for a delivery nobody has been
asked to carry yet. It is the same shape `/orders/{id}/delivery` returns,
so the rider's name, phone and tracking link reach the board in the one
request rather than in one more per card.

LiveOrdersResponse.title: LiveOrdersResponse
LiveOrdersResponse.description: Everything in flight, and what was delivered since `completed_from`.

LiveOrdersStage.title: LiveOrdersStage
LiveOrdersStage.description:
One column of the board.

`total` is how many orders are in this status; `orders` is capped. They
differ on a busy night, and the board says so instead of looking complete.

LiveRestaurantLoad.title: LiveRestaurantLoad
LiveRestaurantLoad.description:
One restaurant's share of the board, counted by the database.

Counted there and not from the cards because the cards are capped: a
restaurant with 213 new orders must not read as 99 because 100 were sent.

detail.title: Detail
detail.default: All sessions have been signed out

LogoutAllResponse.title: LogoutAllResponse
LogoutAllResponse.description: Result of invalidating every session for the calling account.

MarketingCampaignGoal.title: MarketingCampaignGoal
MarketingCampaignGoal.description:
What the owner said they were trying to achieve.

Goals are not rules - they seed defaults (a segment, a set of channels,
whether to suggest a discount) and they label the report. Nothing in the
send path branches on a goal, which is why a new one can be added without
touching dispatch.

MarketingChannel.title: MarketingChannel
MarketingChannel.description:
Delivery channels a campaign can name.

Every value other than PUSH is declared but unsendable in Phase 1. They
exist here because the channel picker has to render them as unavailable
with a reason, and a UI that offers a channel the backend has never heard
of cannot be validated server-side.

MarketingChannelFamily.title: MarketingChannelFamily
MarketingChannelFamily.description:
Whether a channel is addressed to people or broadcast to nobody.

This is the distinction the whole Hub turns on, and it is not cosmetic.

DIRECT (push, WhatsApp, SMS, email) names recipients: consent applies, the
audience is countable before the send, one recipient row is written per
customer, and attribution is measured per recipient from their own send
instant.

SOCIAL (Instagram, Facebook) names nobody. There is no consent to check
and no recipient row to write, so the per-recipient attribution rule the
rest of this product runs on has no subject. A public post is attributed
by a promo code the customer types at checkout, which is a weaker claim
and is reported as one.

MarketingDashboardResponse.title: MarketingDashboardResponse
MarketingDashboardResponse.description: The Hub home's figures, all of them attributed rather than estimated.

MarketingDeepLink.title: MarketingDeepLink
MarketingDeepLink.description: Where tapping the notification lands the customer.

MarketingReferenceResponse.title: MarketingReferenceResponse
MarketingReferenceResponse.description: Everything the wizard needs to render before a draft exists.

MarketingSegmentKey.title: MarketingSegmentKey
MarketingSegmentKey.description:
The audiences a campaign can be sent to.

Each one resolves to a real SQL definition in
`services/marketing/segments.py`; the owner-facing one-liner lives beside
it. They are recency/frequency/monetary shaped, which is deliberately a
different axis from `ai_offer_segments`' item/category/cuisine affinity -
that module answers "what should this offer be about", this one answers
"who should hear from us".

MenuItemPortion.title: MenuItemPortion
MenuItemPortion.description:
Which part of the item a chosen option applies to.

Half-and-half toppings: pepperoni on one side, mushroom on the other. Only
groups the owner marks `supports_halves` may use LEFT or RIGHT, so a client
cannot half-price a topping on an item the kitchen cannot split.

LEFT and RIGHT are labels for two halves, not geometry — the kitchen reads
them off the ticket. Naming them is what lets an order say which topping
goes where at all.

MenuItemStockUpdate.title: MenuItemStockUpdate
MenuItemStockUpdate.description:
The one-tap stock change from the menu list.

Each field is optional and only what is sent is changed, so "mark out of
stock" does not have to know the count and "set the count" does not have
to know whether somebody marked it by hand.

OrderCancelRequest.title: OrderCancelRequest
OrderCancelRequest.description:
A person cancelling: one of the staff reasons, and a note.

The note is required for OTHER_BY_STAFF; `order_cancellation` checks it,
so the rule lives beside the others it belongs with.

OrderCancellationReason.title: OrderCancellationReason
OrderCancellationReason.description:
Why an order was cancelled.

The first four are system-derived. The last five are a person's: since
2026-10-06 the platform admin or the restaurant's owner may cancel an
order the rider has not collected yet (`services/order_cancellation.py`),
choosing one of these, never free text - a note rides beside it.

OrderChargesResponse.title: OrderChargesResponse
OrderChargesResponse.description:
What sits behind "Taxes and charges" when a customer opens it.

One line on the summary, because four extra rows on a checkout read as
nickel-and-diming. A breakdown behind it, because a total nobody can take
apart is a total nobody trusts.

OrderDeliveryResponse.title: OrderDeliveryResponse
OrderDeliveryResponse.description:
What the courier is doing with this order, for the admin.

`state` is ours; `provider_status` is the courier's own word, kept so a
status nobody has seen before is diagnosable from the screen rather than
from the logs. `raw` is deliberately NOT here — it can carry a customer's
address and phone in a shape nothing validates, and the panel has no use
for it.

OrderEventActor.title: OrderEventActor
OrderEventActor.description: Who caused a change: staff, the customer, or an automated job.

OtpRequest.title: OtpRequest
OtpRequest.description: Ask for a code to be sent to a phone number.

OtpRequestResponse.title: OtpRequestResponse
OtpRequestResponse.description: What the client needs to draw the second step of the form.

OtpVerify.title: OtpVerify
OtpVerify.description: Exchange a phone number and a code for a session.

OwnerAIOfferGenerationRequest.title: OwnerAIOfferGenerationRequest
OwnerAIOfferGenerationRequest.description:
An owner's request to generate offers for their own restaurant.

Deliberately has no restaurant field and no `queue_only`: the scope comes
from the signed-in owner, and the run is always inline so the screen can
report a result without a worker attached.

PaymentConfigResponse.title: PaymentConfigResponse
PaymentConfigResponse.description: Client bootstrap. The secret key is never part of this payload.

PaymentGateway.title: PaymentGateway
PaymentGateway.description:
A gateway a restaurant can hold an account with.

Distinct from `PaymentMethod`, which is what the customer picks on the
checkout screen. One gateway can settle several methods — Razorpay's own
checkout covers UPI, cards, netbanking and wallets behind one button — and
one method can be settled by more than one gateway, which is exactly why
these are two enums rather than one.

PaymentGatewayResponse.title: PaymentGatewayResponse
PaymentGatewayResponse.description:
One gateway a restaurant holds an account with.

**No secret appears here, ever.** `secret_last4` is enough to tell two
keys apart when somebody is checking which one is live and useless to
anyone who obtains it; the key itself is Fernet ciphertext that no
endpoint decrypts for a reader.

PaymentLinkResponse.title: PaymentLinkResponse
PaymentLinkResponse.description:
A hosted page to pay one order on. No key, no secret, no card field:
everything sensitive stays on Stripe's side of the link.

PaymentMethodAvailability.title: PaymentMethodAvailability
PaymentMethodAvailability.description:
One checkout button, and whether it is really there.

`is_available` is the answer to the only question the screen is asking:
would a customer standing at this restaurant's checkout right now see this
button. It needs the branch toggle and a working gateway to agree, and
`blocked_reason` says which half is missing rather than leaving an
operator to guess.

PayoutAccountInput.title: PayoutAccountInput
PayoutAccountInput.description:
What the admin types to open a restaurant's linked account.

Checked here in the shape Razorpay checks it, so a typo is caught on this
screen rather than coming back from Razorpay a day later as
NEEDS_CLARIFICATION.

PlatformWatchResponse.title: PlatformWatchResponse
PlatformWatchResponse.description: Is anything wrong, across the whole platform? See `platform_watch`.

PreferenceAnswerInput.title: PreferenceAnswerInput
PreferenceAnswerInput.description: One question's answer. Either chosen options, free text, or both.

PreferenceAnswersPayload.title: PreferenceAnswersPayload
PreferenceAnswersPayload.description: A full submission. Answers omitted for a question clear that question.

PreferenceOptionResponse.title: PreferenceOptionResponse
PreferenceOptionResponse.description: A choice the customer can pick.

PreferenceQuestionResponse.title: PreferenceQuestionResponse
PreferenceQuestionResponse.description: A question, with everything a client needs to render and validate it.

PreferenceSchemaResponse.title: PreferenceSchemaResponse
PreferenceSchemaResponse.description: The whole questionnaire for one app, in the order to ask it.

PreferenceSignalRole.title: PreferenceSignalRole
PreferenceSignalRole.description:
What the recommender is allowed to do with a question's answers.

The questionnaire's structure is data, but its meaning is not: the scoring
engine treats a diet answer differently from a spice answer, and it cannot
infer that from a prompt string. This is the declaration that connects one
to the other.

`NONE` is the important value. A question carrying it is collected, stored
and returned like any other, and contributes nothing to ranking - which is
what lets an owner add a question today without anyone re-tuning the
weights, and what a future taste vector will read from.

PrintJobKind.title: PrintJobKind
PrintJobKind.description:
What a ticket is for.

The kinds are separate because they are different documents with different
audiences, not one document with a flag: a kitchen docket omits money and
shouts the items, a bill shows the money and is handed to a customer, and a
void slip exists to contradict a docket somebody is already holding.

Which printer takes which is `printers.docket_kinds` — data, so one PC can
drive a kitchen printer and a counter printer without the agent branching
on anything.

PrinterTransport.title: PrinterTransport
PrinterTransport.description:
How an agent reaches one printer.

Two, because restaurants have both and the agent is installed into whatever
is already on the counter.

`TCP` is ESC/POS straight to the printer's own address on port 9100. It
needs no driver, produces identical bytes everywhere, and a Windows service
can do it, which is the whole reason it is built first.

`WINDOWS` goes through the print spooler, for a printer attached to the PC
by USB. It carries a constraint that is easy to miss and expensive to
discover: a Windows service runs in Session 0, which has no user profile
and therefore cannot see per-user installed printers. An agent configured
this way has to run as a logged-in user's startup task instead.

RazorpayCheckoutConfirm.title: RazorpayCheckoutConfirm
RazorpayCheckoutConfirm.description:
The three values Razorpay Checkout hands the browser on success.

Worth nothing until verified: the signature is an HMAC of the other two
with the restaurant's API secret, which is what makes them believable.

ResolvedAddress.title: ResolvedAddress
ResolvedAddress.description: A place the customer chose, in the shape the checkout form uses.

RestaurantBrandResponse.title: RestaurantBrandResponse
RestaurantBrandResponse.description: What this restaurant says about itself, and the room it has to say it.

RestaurantBrandUpdate.title: RestaurantBrandUpdate
RestaurantBrandUpdate.description:
The long-form content on a restaurant's own website.

Both halves optional, and only the ones sent are changed — an edit to the
FAQ must not blank the about sections. Sending a key as an empty list
clears that half, which is a deliberate act and a different one from not
mentioning it.

Length and shape rules belong to `restaurant_brand.py`, so they are the
same wherever this is written rather than half here and half there.

RestaurantCapabilityResponse.title: RestaurantCapabilityResponse
RestaurantCapabilityResponse.description:
One capability, as both screens render it.

`reason` and `explanation` are not decoration. A capability that is off
with nothing saying why is the exact state that made the allowlist this
system replaced harmful — see `config/capabilities.py`.

RestaurantCapabilityUpdate.title: RestaurantCapabilityUpdate
RestaurantCapabilityUpdate.description:
Switch one capability, or hand it back to the default.

`enabled: null` clears the decision rather than storing "off" — an
operator who granted something as a one-off should be able to say "treat
this like everyone else" without pinning today's default in place.

RestaurantLocationGeneralSettingsUpdate.title: RestaurantLocationGeneralSettingsUpdate
RestaurantLocationGeneralSettingsUpdate.description:
What the branch's settings form may change.

`extra="forbid"`, and that is the important line. Pydantic's default is to
DROP a field it does not recognise, so this endpoint answered 200 and saved
nothing when the form learned to send the charge rates before this schema
learned to accept them — the admin showed "saved", reloaded, and displayed
the old values, with nothing in any log.

A settings endpoint that quietly ignores half of what it was sent is worse
than one that refuses: the refusal is a 422 somebody fixes in a minute,
while the silence is a bug reported as "it does not save".

RestaurantPaymentGatewayUpdate.title: RestaurantPaymentGatewayUpdate
RestaurantPaymentGatewayUpdate.description:
Store or update one gateway's credentials.

`secret_key` and `webhook_secret` of null mean "leave what is there". The
screen cannot show a stored secret, so it submits nothing whenever nobody
retyped one — and treating that as "clear it" would wipe a live gateway
every time an operator toggled it off and on.

RestaurantStorefrontResponse.title: RestaurantStorefrontResponse
RestaurantStorefrontResponse.description: What this restaurant's website says, and what it would say by itself.

RestaurantStorefrontUpdate.title: RestaurantStorefrontUpdate
RestaurantStorefrontUpdate.description:
The restaurant's own words for its website.

Every field optional, and only the ones sent are changed — a form that
edits the hero must not blank the meta description. Sending a field as an
empty string clears it, which means "go back to the derived default"
rather than "this restaurant's hero has no words".

Validation of length and shape belongs to `restaurant_storefront.py`, so
the rules are the same wherever copy is written, rather than half here and
half there.

RestaurantThemeResponse.title: RestaurantThemeResponse
RestaurantThemeResponse.description: The restaurant's look, plus the gallery to pick from.

RestaurantThemeUpdate.title: RestaurantThemeUpdate
RestaurantThemeUpdate.description: Either a named preset or a custom colour; the preset wins if both come.

SocialPostResponse.title: SocialPostResponse
SocialPostResponse.description:
The public post a social campaign produced.

Null for every direct campaign, and the two are never both populated: a
campaign is a message to people or a post to nobody.

SuggestRequest.title: SuggestRequest
SuggestRequest.description: What the customer has typed so far.

SuggestionOfferActivationResponse.title: SuggestionOfferActivationResponse
SuggestionOfferActivationResponse.description: The end state of an offer a chat card started.

TenantStatusUpdate.title: TenantStatusUpdate
TenantStatusUpdate.description:
A lifecycle change, with the sentence explaining it.

`note` is required for anything other than reactivation. A tenant whose
storefront stops answering generates a support call within the hour, and
"who turned this off and why" should be answerable from the record rather
than from memory.

TenantSummaryResponse.title: TenantSummaryResponse
TenantSummaryResponse.description: One tenant as the operator's console lists it.

TestSendRequest.title: TestSendRequest
TestSendRequest.description:
Campaign copy, sent to the staff member asking for it and nobody else.

Carries the text rather than a campaign id so the wizard can test a draft
that has not been saved — which is the moment an owner actually wants to
see it on a phone.

`channel` defaults to push so a client written before the other channels
existed keeps working. A social channel is refused rather than defaulted:
there is no private way to test a public post, and quietly sending a push
instead would let an owner conclude Instagram works.

UserProfileUpdateRequest.title: UserProfileUpdateRequest
UserProfileUpdateRequest.description:
A PATCH, and now it behaves like one.

**Every field used to be written unconditionally**, so a field left out of
the body was stored as NULL. `api.updateProfile` sends only `full_name` and
`phone_number` — so a customer who edited their name on the account screen
silently lost their saved delivery address, every time. It was found
because a test fixture's address kept disappearing between runs.

The rule is the one `services/restaurant_storefront.py` already uses for
the same reason: **only the keys actually present in the body change.**
Pydantic records which those were in `model_fields_set`, which is the only
way to tell "not mentioned" from "sent as null" — the two had the same
representation here, and conflating them is the bug.

So: absent leaves a field alone, and an explicit `null` clears it. The
account screen already sends `phone_number: null` when the customer empties
that box, so it means exactly what it did before; it simply no longer takes
the address with it.

`full_name` is optional because a PATCH should not demand a field you are
not changing — but it cannot be CLEARED, because the column is NOT NULL and
an account with no name is not a thing this product has. Sending it as null
or blank is refused rather than ignored, since a client that asks to erase
a name should hear that it did not happen.

UserRegister.title: UserRegister
UserRegister.description:
Public registration always creates a CUSTOMER.

The role used to be taken from the request body, which let anyone
self-register as ADMIN. Staff accounts are created through admin-only
endpoints instead. Clients already send `role: "CUSTOMER"`; the extra field
is simply ignored.

UserResponse.title: UserResponse
UserResponse.description:
An account as stored, for reading back.

Not `UserBase`: its rules (a two-letter name, an email that validates,
an eight-digit phone) are for what somebody types at sign-up. A customer
who signed in by phone OTP had no name yet, and inheriting them turned
`GET /admin/users` into a 500 for every admin - which a browser reports
as a CORS error. What is stored is shown as it is.
